strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem for an under-resourced language (Hausa), targeting orthographic variations and digital writing anomalies that frequently degrade NLP tool performance.
Methodology for synthetic noise generation is thoughtfully calibrated against real-world data (10,000 Hausa tweets) to match empirical Levenshtein distance distributions.

Comprehensive empirical benchmarking across multiple pretrained multilingual and African-centric seq2seq architectures (M2M100, AfriTEVA variants, mBART, mT5, Opus-MT), evaluated using multiple string- and token-level metrics (BLEU, METEOR, F1, WER, CER).

Provides both a quantitative human evaluation on 500 samples and a candid qualitative error analysis in the appendix illustrating failure modes such as named-entity drift and catastrophic hallucinations on technical texts.
weaknesses: Evaluation is performed almost entirely on synthetic test data generated with the same noise process as the training set; there is no quantitative benchmark on an authentic, manually annotated corpus of real-world noisy Hausa text.

Lacks simple and interpretable non-neural baselines (such as rule-based lookup for hooked characters or n-gram language model beam search), making it difficult to isolate the net gain of heavy seq2seq models over simpler normalization techniques.
Human evaluation is conducted by only a single native speaker without inter-annotator agreement metrics.
No downstream extrinsic evaluation is provided to verify whether the proposed normalization actually improves downstream tasks like machine translation, NER, or sentiment analysis.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem for an under-resourced language: orthographic normalization and typo correction for Hausa, particularly handling hooked consonants (ɓ, ɗ, ƙ, ƴ) and spacing anomalies common in digital text.

Comprehensive empirical comparison across diverse model families and scales, including multilingual seq2seq models (M2M100, mBART, mT5), dedicated African language models (AfriTEVA, AfriMBART), and translation architectures (Opus-MT).
Synthetic noise generation is systematically calibrated against real Twitter data by aligning normalized Levenshtein distance distributions.
Includes qualitative error analysis and a native-speaker evaluation of 500 outputs to complement automated string overlap and edit distance metrics.
weaknesses: The evaluation is conducted entirely on synthetically corrupted data. Because the models are evaluated on test sets generated with the exact same noise functions used during training, high performance may reflect memorization of the noise heuristics rather than true robustness on natural, noisy Hausa text. Evaluating on a gold-standard benchmark of naturally occurring noisy sentences (e.g., annotated tweets) is needed.

The human evaluation was performed on outputs originating from synthetic inputs rather than authentic social media text, and relies on a single annotator without inter-annotator agreement or standardized error categorization.

Lack of standard non-neural and heuristic baselines: since the dominant errors are specific hooked-letter substitutions and spacing issues, simple rule-based, dictionary-based, or n-gram language model baselines should be included to contextualize the benefits of heavy transformer models.

Several models exhibit extreme failure modes (e.g., AfriMBART achieves a CER of 2.717 and AfriTEVA-Large degrades to a WER of 1.044), but the paper offers little diagnostic insight or ablation into why these specific pre-trained representations fail so severely on this task.

No downstream task evaluation: while the introduction strongly argues that writing anomalies harm downstream Hausa NLP applications (e.g., sentiment analysis or machine translation), no experiments are conducted to verify whether pre-processing noisy data with the proposed model actually yields downstream performance gains.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical bottleneck in Hausa NLP, specifically orthographic anomalies (such as hooked characters ɓ, ɗ, ƙ, ƴ being replaced by standard Latin letters) and spacing irregularities.

The synthetic noise generation is thoughtfully calibrated by matching the normalized Levenshtein distance distribution of authentic Hausa tweets, rather than applying completely arbitrary perturbations.
Compares a broad suite of multilingual and African-centric pretrained seq2seq models (M2M100, AfriTEVA, Opus-MT, mT5, mBART) alongside an LSTM baseline.
Includes qualitative error analysis and a human evaluation assessing the preservation of core semantics and specific failure modes (e.g., named entity transliterations).
weaknesses: The quantitative evaluation is conducted entirely on synthetic test data generated by the exact same noise functions and parameter distributions used for training data generation, which inherently risks overfitting to the synthetic corruption process and overestimating real-world performance.

There is no evaluation on a benchmark of naturally occurring Hausa errors (e.g., manually annotated social media text) to demonstrate how well the model generalizes to genuine typos, dialectal noise, and informal writing.
The technical and algorithmic novelty is limited, as the work primarily applies standard sequence-to-sequence fine-tuning with existing architectures on synthetically corrupted parallel sentences.

The motivation claims significant benefits for downstream NLP applications (such as machine translation or sentiment analysis), but the paper provides no extrinsic downstream evaluation to validate whether preprocessing text with the proposed pipeline actually yields downstream improvements.
Several model behaviors lack sufficient diagnostic investigation—for instance, why AfriTEVA-Large and AfriMBART collapsed (WER > 1.0 / CER > 2.0) while AfriTEVA-Base performed relatively well.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in Hausa NLP: orthographic variation, segmentation/spacing inconsistencies, and missing hooked characters (ɓ, ɗ, ƙ, ƴ) that frequently degrade downstream model performance.

The noise injection method is well motivated and grounded: rather than applying arbitrary noise, the error distribution and edit distances are calibrated against real-world social media data (NaijaSenti) using Jensen–Shannon divergence.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across a diverse suite of architectures (monolingual/multilingual African models, seq2seq translation models like M2M100, and instruction-tuned LLMs like N-ATLaS 8B), complemented by an out-of-domain evaluation and a 500-instance human analysis.

Extensive downstream validation showing how automated normalization impacts text classification, machine translation (FLORES+), and structured reasoning / zero-shot LLM benchmarks (IrokoBench, MasakhaNER).
weaknesses: Both the in-domain and out-of-domain test sets rely on synthetically injected noise rather than genuine human-annotated noisy texts. While downstream experiments partly bridge this gap, having even a small gold evaluation set of authentic noisy Hausa texts with human reference corrections would significantly strengthen the empirical claims.

Font encoding / rendering issue: across several sections (e.g., Introduction, Section 3, Section 5.1), Hausa-specific hooked characters are rendered as blank spaces in parentheses (e.g., '( , , , and )'), hindering readability and precision.

References to proprietary LLM versions ('GPT-5.1' and 'GPT-5.4') appear anomalous or speculative, which impairs transparency and reproducibility regarding the exact closed-source model configurations used for baseline comparisons.

strengths: Addresses an important, practical bottleneck in African language technology: orthographic irregularity, loss of special Hausa hooked characters (ɓ, ɗ, ƙ, ƴ), and spacing anomalies in digital text.

The noise simulation methodology is principled and well-motivated: rather than choosing arbitrary noise rates, the authors calibrate character and token mutation probabilities against empirical edit distances from the NaijaSenti Twitter corpus, verified via Jensen–Shannon divergence.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple model families (multilingual seq2seq like M2M100, Africa-centric models like AfriTeVA and Cheetah, and instruction-tuned LLMs like N-ATLaS), providing actionable findings regarding the cost-efficiency of compact translation models versus 8B models.

Broad downstream task validation across text genre classification, machine translation (FLORES+), and instruction-following/reasoning tasks (MasakhaNER, AfriMMLU, AfriMGSM, AfriXNLI), demonstrating the concrete utility of text normalization pipelines.
weaknesses: The correction models are evaluated exclusively on synthetically corrupted data. While the noise distribution is calibrated to empirical Twitter statistics, there is no intrinsic evaluation on authentic, naturally occurring noisy Hausa text (e.g., raw tweets or informal web corpora) with human-annotated gold corrections.

Font rendering/compilation issues: throughout the manuscript (e.g., Sections 1, 3, 5.1), special Hausa characters are missing in parentheses (rendered as empty whitespace between commas), which should be fixed to ensure readability.
Human evaluation is conducted by only a single native speaker on 500 samples without measuring inter-annotator agreement or providing a multi-annotator validation framework.

Inconsistencies and non-standard model nomenclature (e.g., referencing 'GPT-5.1' in Section 4/5 and 'GPT-5.4' in Section 6.3), which appear to be either speculative version names, placeholders, or typos that distract from the technical rigor.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical bottleneck in Hausa NLP: digital writing anomalies, diacritic/hooked character substitutions, and word boundary/spacing errors.

Methodologically sound noise-induction strategy: rather than injecting arbitrary noise, the error distribution and probabilities are calibrated against naturally occurring noisy tweets (NaijaSenti) using edit-distance clustering and Jensen-Shannon divergence validation.
Extensive experimental comparison covering a diverse suite of multilingual and African-specific language models (e.g., M2M100, AfriTeVA, Cheetah, N-ATLaS).

Thorough evaluation protocol including both in-domain and out-of-domain test sets, native-speaker human evaluation of 500 samples, and downstream evaluations on classification, machine translation (FLORES+), and instruction-following/reasoning benchmarks (IrokoBench).
weaknesses: Font/rendering errors throughout the manuscript: Hausa-specific hooked characters are missing entirely (appearing as empty spaces in brackets, e.g., on page 1, 4, and 6), which degrades reading quality and obscures exact orthographic definitions.

Evaluation relies entirely on synthetically noised test data: although synthetic noise is calibrated against Twitter distributions, the paper does not evaluate correction performance on a dedicated gold-standard benchmark of naturally occurring, human-annotated noisy-clean Hausa sentence pairs.

Unclear model nomenclature: references to proprietary models named 'GPT-5.1' and 'GPT-5.4' without clear versioning, snapshot dates, or documentation undermine clarity and experimental reproducibility.

Downstream tasks are also evaluated on synthetically degraded benchmark data rather than inherently noisy real-world data (e.g., raw social media text), and for some tasks like genre classification, the observed differences between noisy and cleaned text fall within overlapping error margins.
